{{Use mdy dates|date=November 2021}}{{Use American English|date=November 2021}}
'''William Gaylord Conway''' (November 20, 1929{{snd}}October 21, 2021) was an American [[zoologist]], [[ornithologist]] and [[conservation movement|conservationist]].

William Gaylord Conway was born on November 20, 1929, in [[St. Louis]], Missouri.<ref name="nytobit">{{Cite news|last=Roberts|first=Sam|author-link=Sam Roberts (newspaper journalist)|date=2021-11-05|title=William Conway, Who Reimagined America's Zoos, Is Dead at 91|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/11/05/nyregion/william-conway-dead.html|access-date=2021-11-06|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

He began his career with the [[St. Louis Zoo]]. He joined the [[New York Zoological Society]] in 1956 as assistant curator of birds. He was later promoted to director of the society, and then became president of it in 1992 when it was reconfigured into the [[Wildlife Conservation Society]]. He retired as president in 1999 and retained the title of senior conservationist.<ref name="ADN">{{Cite book | url=https://archive.org/details/differentnaturep0000hanc/page/105 | title=A Different Nature: The Paradoxical World of Zoos and Their Uncertain Future | author=David Hancocks | publisher=University of California Press | page=[https://archive.org/details/differentnaturep0000hanc/page/105 105] | year=2002 | isbn=0-520-23676-9 }}</ref>

During his tenure, Conway was responsible for modernizing the animal exhibits at the [[Bronx Zoo]], and he also introduced now iconic Bronx Zoo exhibits, including the World of Darkness (1969), the World of Birds (1972), Wild Asia (1977), JungleWorld (1985), and Congo Gorilla Forest (1999).<ref name=ADN/> Conway was a proponent of zoological exhibition of animals in a setting that recreated the environment from which the species originated.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/animalattraction0000hans |url-access=registration |quote=william conway bronx zoo. | title=Animal Attractions: Nature on Display in American Zoos |author=Elizabeth Hanson | publisher=Princeton University Press | pages=[https://archive.org/details/animalattraction0000hans/page/176 176]–7 | year=2002 | isbn=0-691-05992-6}}</ref>

Conway successfully negotiated the society's acquisition of the [[Central Park Zoo]] from the [[New York City]] municipal government in 1981, which resulted in an extensive renovation program for the attraction so it could meet modern zoological exhibition requirements.<ref>{{cite news | author =Robert Beninder | title =It's All Happening at the Zoo | publisher =City Journal | date =Summer 1993 | url =http://www.city-journal.org/article02.php?aid=1483 | access-date =2009-10-23 | archive-date =July 3, 2010 | archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20100703082738/http://www.city-journal.org/article02.php?aid=1483 | url-status =dead }}</ref>

Conway has also been in the forefront of promoting [[captive breeding]] programs for [[endangered species]]. He was responsible for creating the Wildlife Propagation Trust in 1964, that resulted in the coordination of zoos to pursue the twin goals of preserving at-risk species and eventually reintroducing animals back to the wild.<ref>{{cite news | title =Survival Centers for Rare Animals | publisher =Life Magazine  | date =August 21, 1964 | url =https://books.google.com/books?id=ZkkEAAAAMBAJ&dq=%22william+conway%22+%22bronx+zoo%22&pg=PA45 | access-date=2009-10-23}}</ref>

Conway appeared as himself on May 7, 1962 episode of the [[CBS]] game show ''[[To Tell the Truth]]''.<ref>{{cite web |title=To Tell the Truth |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Z8i6WtsCg7s |website=[[CBS]] |access-date=14 February 2026}}</ref>

Conway was also responsible for leading the development of the [[American Zoo and Aquarium Association]] accreditation program. He has authored more than 250 articles and reports relating to wildlife conservation, [[ornithology]], wild animal care propagation and ecological preservation.

In 1999, the [[National Audubon Society]] awarded Conway its highest honor, the Audubon Medal.

Conway died on October 21, 2021, in [[New Rochelle, New York]].<ref name="nytobit" />
